cited_details.statement: Person search aims to localize and re-identify a target individual from a large gallery of unconstrained scene images, and has become a critical capability for public-safety and social-governance applications such as video surveillance, missing-person retrieval, and forensic search [Xiao et al., 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850).

The query may take two forms—an image (image-based person search) or a natural-language description (text-based person search) [Shah & Vuong, 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.00365); [Zhou et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08923).

The query may take two forms—an image (image-based person search) or a natural-language description (text-based person search) [Shah & Vuong, 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.00365); [Zhou et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08923).
The query is a cropped image of the target; the system must return the bounding boxes of that identity across a gallery of full scene images [Xiao et al., 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850).

The dominant benchmark is CUHK-SYSU, which contains 18,184 images and 8,432 distinct identities collected from street photography and movies [CUHK-SYSU dataset description](https://hyper.ai/en/datasets/17981); a complementary benchmark is PRW, also used for end-to-end evaluation [Loesch et al., 2019](https://cea.hal.science/cea-03251768/document).

(2017) and Shah & Vuong (2018) demonstrated that attention-based and reinforcement-learning-based alignment mechanisms are central to handling this cross-modal setting [Zhou et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08923); [Shah & Vuong, 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.00365).

(2016) argue that the detection and re-identification sub-networks should share a common convolutional encoder, since the representation learned for one sub-task is informative for the other; they couple a Faster R-CNN-style detector with an identification head trained by the Online Instance Matching (OIM) loss, which is robust to the sparse, unbalanced labels that arise when supervising scene-level person search [Xiao et al., 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850).

(2020) extend OIM with a triplet formulation, mining hard positive/negative pairs online so that the embedding forms compact, well-separated identity clusters [Li et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10560).

At a more structural level, Multi-Level Joint Feature Learning combines global holistic descriptors with local part-based features, arguing that fine-grained cues such as logos and garment patches complement the global body shape and yield more discriminative embeddings [Multi-Level Joint Feature Learning, 2020](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4893/13/5/111).

For text-based retrieval, the representation problem becomes cross-modal: visual and linguistic features must be embedded into a common space in which identity-bearing regions of the image correspond to identity-bearing phrases of the text [Zhou et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08923).

The broader multimodal-representation literature confirms that the choice between joint, coordinated, and encoder–decoder integration frameworks has profound effects on how the heterogeneity gap is narrowed [Deep Multimodal Representation Learning Survey, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2019.2916887).

Siamese and triplet networks are the dominant architectural templates, and the design of structured losses plus informative pair-mining strategies is a recurring theme [Deep Metric Learning Survey, 2019](https://doi.org/10.3390/sym11091066).

(2016) provide a non-parametric instance-level metric by maintaining a circular queue of labeled identity prototypes and a circular queue of unlabeled features, then computing a soft classification over both; this functions as an efficient similarity over the gallery without requiring a parametric classifier head [Xiao et al., 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850).

(2020) show that augmenting OIM with a triplet loss simultaneously reduces intra-class variance and increases inter-class margin, outperforming softmax-only OIM on CUHK-SYSU [Li et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10560).

The identity-regression framework embeds each pedestrian as a point in a continuous identity latent space and turns matching into nearest-neighbor search, which is reported to scale gracefully to large populations and to adapt to gradual appearance drift [Person Re-identification in Identity Regression Space, 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6411216/).

Shah & Vuong (2018) use deep reinforcement learning to learn a policy that decides where to attend on both the image and the text, iteratively refining the cross-modal alignment without requiring rigid phrase-region correspondences [Shah & Vuong, 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.00365).
(2017) instead apply learned attention to both encoders so that the similarity score emphasizes identity-bearing words and image regions [Zhou et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08923).

These approaches fit naturally into the broader taxonomy of deep metric learning, where the success of a Siamese or triplet architecture depends critically on the loss and sampling strategy [Deep Metric Learning Survey, 2019](https://doi.org/10.3390/sym11091066).

The third challenge is unique to end-to-end person search: pedestrian detection and re-identification are typically trained with different objectives (bounding-box classification/regression versus identity classification), and naively sharing parameters can be suboptimal because the two tasks favor different feature statistics [Xiao et al., 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850).

The OIM framework addresses this through a single CNN that produces both detection proposals and re-id embeddings, with identity supervision that is robust to sparse and unbalanced labels [Xiao et al., 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01850).

(2019) investigate training schedules for end-to-end person search on both CUHK-SYSU and PRW, and report that the balance between detection and identification losses—as well as the order in which the two sub-tasks are unfrozen during training—materially affects the final accuracy, confirming that identity-driven detection is not merely a matter of architecture but also of optimization [Loesch et al., 2019](https://cea.hal.science/cea-03251768/document).

evidence.title: Deep Multimodal Representation Learning: A Survey
evidence.abstract: Multimodal representation learning, which aims to narrow the heterogeneity gap among different modalities, plays an indispensable role in the utilization of ubiquitous multimodal data. Due to the powerful representation ability with multiple levels of abstraction, deep learning-based multimodal representation learning has attracted much attention in recent years. In this paper, we provided a comprehensive survey on deep multimodal representation learning which has never been concentrated entirely. To facilitate the discussion on how the heterogeneity gap is narrowed, according to the underlying structures in which different modalities are integrated, we category deep multimodal representation learning methods into three frameworks: joint representation, coordinated representation, and encoder-decoder. Additionally, we review some typical models in this area ranging from conventional models to newly developed technologies. This paper highlights on the key issues of newly developed technologies, such as encoder-decoder model, generative adversarial networks, and attention mechanism in a multimodal representation learning perspective, which, to the best of our knowledge, have never been reviewed previously, even though they have become the major focuses of much contemporary research. For each framework or model, we discuss its basic structure, learning objective, application scenes, key issues, advantages, and disadvantages, such that both novel and experienced researchers can benefit from this survey. Finally, we suggest some important directions for future work.

evidence.title: Natural Language Person Search Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
evidence.abstract: Recent success in deep reinforcement learning is having an agent learn how to play Go and beat the world champion without any prior knowledge of the game. In that task, the agent has to make a decision on what action to take based on the positions of the pieces. Person Search is recently explored using natural language based text description of images for video surveillance applications (S.Li et.al). We see (Fu.et al) provides an end to end approach for object-based retrieval using deep reinforcement learning without constraints placed on which objects are being detected. However, we believe for real-world applications such as person search defining specific constraints which identify a person as opposed to starting with a general object detection will have benefits in terms of performance and computational resources required. In our task, Deep reinforcement learning would localize the person in an image by reshaping the sizes of the bounding boxes. Deep Reinforcement learning with appropriate constraints would look only for the relevant person in the image as opposed to an unconstrained approach where each individual objects in the image are ranked. For person search, the agent is trying to form a tight bounding box around the person in the image who matches the description. The bounding box is initialized to the full image and at each time step, the agent makes a decision on how to change the current bounding box so that it has a tighter bound around the person based on the description of the person and the pixel values of the current bounding box. After the agent takes an action, it will be given a reward based on the Intersection over Union (IoU) of the current bounding box and the ground truth box. Once the agent believes that the bounding box is covering the person, it will indicate that the person is found.
